body.text: United States President Donald Trump's approval rating is at a record low less than a month away from the 3 November midterm elections, but experts warn against calling the result.
A new Reuters/Ipsos poll on Monday found 32 per cent of Americans approve of his presidency, unchanged from September's career low.

Among those who have drifted away are Hispanic Americans, with approval sitting at just 24 per cent, the lowest in either of his terms. Trump won nearly half the Hispanic vote in 2024, up from roughly a third in 2020.
The polling also suggested Trump's low popularity was weighing heavily on his Republican Party, with registered voters preferring Democrats over Republicans by 44 per cent to 37 per cent.

Among older voters, who have typically been a Republican stronghold, support is dwindling. Voters aged 50 and over still preferred Republicans — but just by 2 percentage points (44 per cent to 42 per cent) — compared to an eight-point Republican advantage last December.
Those under 50 favour Democrats by 18.
It's not the only polling suggesting support for Trump is fading.
An NBC News poll of 1,000 registered voters from 11-15 September suggested just 41 per cent approve of Trump, while 56 per cent disapprove of him — a second-term low in their poll.
Half of those surveyed (50 per cent) preferred Democratic control of Congress, while 45 per cent preferred Republican control.
Meanwhile, Economist/YouGov polling from 25-28 September found 36 per cent approved of Trump and 62 per cent disapproved.
The New York Times, which has aggregated more than 1,000 polls since Inauguration Day, now places his approval rating at 37 per cent and disapproval at 60 per cent.
Trump's big problem
Pollsters and analysts point to the same culprit: the cost of living.
Cost of living is the top issue on Americans' minds as they decide how they will vote next month, the Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
Consumer inflation has spiked following a surge in gasoline and diesel prices brought on by the war with Iran that Trump launched in February.

When asked what the most important problem facing the US today was, Economist/YouGov respondents leaned towards the economy: 29 per cent answered inflation, 14 per cent the economy, and 10 per cent presidential leadership.
Pew Research found 29 per cent of voters spontaneously named an economic concern when asked what they most wanted congressional candidates to discuss — more than three times any other category.
Another survey, from the Joseph Rainey Centre for Public Policy, found 57 per cent placing groceries, gas or utilities among their top three issues.
Trump's tariffs feed directly into the debate, with opponents blaming them for higher costs while the administration argues they protect American industry and raise revenue.
But Jared Mondschein, director of research at the United States Studies Centre, says the pattern is not new.
"The percentage of Americans who say that the economy is the number one issue has remained consistent since 2022," Mondschein told SBS News, adding that it has held at about a third.

"More than anything else, it was economic problems in 2024 that won Donald Trump the election," he said. "In many ways, it's the number one problem that is leading to record-low approval ratings for him right now."
Around 55 per cent of registered voters told NBC News that Trump's policies had hurt the economy, against 26 per cent who said they had helped it.
'Not a normal election'
A Wall Street Journal survey found no president heading into the midterms had polled worse in its surveys dating to 1990.
But experts are still hesitant to call the election.
Emma Shortis, director of international and security at the left-wing thinktank The Australia Institute, is reluctant to make predictions about the outcome, even amid record-low polling.
"There are just so many moving parts in this cycle that it's very difficult to know how they might all fit together or not fit together," she told SBS News.

"In a 'normal' electoral cycle, we would expect to see a catastrophic loss for Republicans — on current polling, they are looking at the loss of the House and potentially the loss of the Senate, which would be enormous."
"But this is not a normal election."
Over the past year, Republicans and Democrats have sought to redraw electoral boundary lines to suit them, known as gerrymandering.
Mondschein questions how much polling can reveal at all. "I can tell you where the polling is, but the polling is always wrong," he said.
He points to early in the 2016 cycle, when polling had Jeb Bush and Scott Walker as the Republican frontrunners.
"Donald Trump was nowhere near being competitive at this time in the 2016 race, and then he ends up being the most impactful Republican candidate for a few decades," Mondschein said.
A 'referendum' on Trump
Trump has spent much of his campaign encouraging Republicans to "pretend" he is on the ballot, arguing that voters should view the midterms as a referendum on his administration and economic record.
Shortis agrees that the vote is a referendum of sorts.
"This will be a referendum on Trump's particular version of conservatism," she said.
But she cautioned against underestimating his "ability to recover politically".
"We know he's very good at that."
Mondschein says the risk for Trump is that he isn't energising the voters his party needs.
"He is alienating — or perhaps not energising — the voters who he needs to energise for this midterm election be competitive."
Who's on the ballot
That's why, despite the national numbers, Mondschein says the outcome will turn on individual candidates rather than parties.
"Democrats and Republicans are not on the ballot — individuals are on the ballot," he said.

He points to Republicans in states that should be a surefire win, like Texas, North Carolina and Georgia, who are doing worse than a Republican in Michigan, which has voted Democrat more often than not over the past decade.
Democrats are now competitive in Senate races in Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska — states Trump won by double digits in 2024.
But Democrats shouldn't assume the tide is theirs, he warned.
"I think Democrats would be making a mistake to think that somehow they are seen as favourably as much as they are increasingly seen as less unfavourably than Republicans."
"At the end of the day, it really depends on who is on the ballot."
Trump, for his part, insists the polls are wrong.
"I think we're going to have a big surprise because they don't know what's happening," he told a rally in Ohio on Saturday.
Mondschein puts it more bluntly: "Every time that we try to predict a future of a party, we seem to get it wrong."
— With additional reporting by Reuters and Agence France-Presse.
